	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true

In the mild and moderate groups, IL-6 concentrations were at their highest level in the first week after the symptom onset and then exhibited a decreasing trend.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

In the mild and moderate groups, IL-6 concentrations were at their highest level in the first week after the symptom onset and then exhibited a decreasing trend.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing

	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators

	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true

greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c

d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species

The temporal_operators are:

- eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate): between t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate is true for the rest of the interval.

- globally[t_a,t_b](phi): the predicate is true over the entire interval from t_a to t_b.

- eventually[t_a,t_b](phi): there is at least one time between t_a and t_b that the predicate is true.

But if you want to say that there exists a time in [1,7] where the predicate is true for the rest of the interval, then it's "eventually[1,7]globally(predicate)".

thinking prompt: Give an explanation of how you would translate the following natural language sentence into a signal temporal logic (STL) statement:
Remarkably, in the mild group, the amount of these cytokines (IL-1β and IL-1Ra) increased at the day 1–7, reached a peak at the day 8–14, and diminished after >14 days.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

- globally[t_a,t_b](predicate): the predicate is true over the entire interval from t_a to t_b.

- eventually[t_a,t_b](predicate): there is at least one point in t_a to t_b where the predicate is true.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c

	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days

	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing

	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true

TNF-α levels elevated at the day 1–7 and 8–14 times intervals, then decreased at the day>14.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c

	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use

greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c

	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days

thinking prompt: Give an explanation of how you would translate the following natural language sentence into a signal temporal logic (STL) statement:
We detected that IL-8 was significantly elevated in all COVID-19 subgroups at three studied time intervals compared to the control group.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

Now, translating into STL. STL uses temporal operators like eventually, globally, etc., and comparisons with species' levels.

First, the part about day 1–7: "no difference in production of IFN-β" implies that the levels are equal between patients and controls. So, for the first interval, we can use the 'is' operator for equality. But since the time is a range (day 1–7), we need to specify that the predicate holds throughout that interval.

Starting with the first part: "We found that although there was no difference..." This is a contrast. In STL, we can use 'eventually' or 'globally' with negations. But since it's a contrast, maybe using 'eventually' for the negative part.

Then, the second part: "IFN-β levels were higher in moderate, severe, and critical subjects at the day 8–14 or >14 compared to the healthy control and themselves at the day 1–7."

So, the comparison is between the patients (with COVID-19) and the healthy control group, and the patients themselves at day 1-7.

So, the STL statement would need to capture that at day 8-14 or >14, the level of IFN-β is higher than the healthy control and the patients' levels at day 1-7.

But how to structure this. Let's think about the time intervals. The first part is day 1-7, and the second part is day 8-14 and >14. So, the overall statement is that for the time interval starting at day 1-7, the patients have a certain level, but then after day 7, their levels increase.

- For the time interval [1,7], the level of IFN-β is equal to the healthy control (since no difference).
- For the time interval [8,14] and [15, ...], the level of IFN-β is higher than the healthy control and the patients' levels at [1,7].

We found that although there was no difference in the production of IFN-β in all patients with COVID-19 compared to the control group at the day 1–7, IFN-β levels were higher in moderate, severe, and critical subjects at the day 8–14 or >14 compared to the healthy control and themselves at the day 1–7.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

First, I need to parse the original sentence. The key parts are:

1. "We found that although there was no difference in the production of IFN-β in all patients with COVID-19 compared to the control group at the day 1–7, IFN-β levels were higher in moderate, severe, and critical subjects at the day 8–14 or >14 compared to the healthy control and themselves at the day 1–7."

So, the main points are:

- No difference in production (IFN-β) from day 1-7 between patients and controls.
- Higher levels in moderate, severe, critical patients at days 8-14 or >14 compared to healthy controls and themselves on day 1-7.

Now, translating into STL. STL uses temporal operators like eventually, globally, etc., and comparison operators like <, >, =.

First, the first part: "no difference in the production of IFN-β in all patients with COVID-19 compared to the control group at day 1–7." This translates to the levels being equal (is) between patients and controls on day 1-7. So, for the species IFNβ, the level on days 1-7 is equal between patients and controls.

Then, the second part: "IFN-β levels were higher in moderate, severe, and critical subjects at the day 8–14 or >14 compared to the healthy control and themselves at the day 1–7." 

Here, the comparison is between the levels on days 8-14 or >14 (moderate, severe, critical) vs. healthy control and themselves (patients and controls on day 1-7). 

But wait, the original says "compared to the healthy control and themselves at the day 1–7." So, the subjects (moderate, severe, critical) have higher levels on days 8-14 or >14 compared to the healthy control (which is a different group) and themselves (the same patients and controls on day 1-7).

So, for the days 8-14 or >14, the levels of IFNβ are higher than the healthy control and also higher than their own levels on day 1-7.

So maybe it's written as: for the interval [1,7], the level of IFNβ is equal to the control group. So, perhaps using the 'is' operator with the control group.

But the control group is a specific group. Wait, the original mentions "control group" and "healthy control". So, the healthy control is a separate group. So, the healthy control is a different group than the patients. Therefore, the first part is that for days 1-7, the level of IFNβ is equal between patients and the healthy control. Wait, no. Wait, the original says "compared to the control group at the day 1–7". So, the control group is the healthy control? Or is the control group the non-patient group?

Wait, the original sentence says "all patients with COVID-19 compared to the control group". So, the control group is the healthy individuals. [BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is

	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true

thinking prompt: Give an explanation of how you would translate the following natural language sentence into a signal temporal logic (STL) statement:
We found that although there was no difference in the production of IFN-β in all patients with COVID-19 compared to the control group at the day 1–7, IFN-β levels were higher in moderate, severe, and critical subjects at the day 8–14 or >14 compared to the healthy control and themselves at the day 1–7.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

We found that although there was no difference in the production of IFN-β in all patients with COVID-19 compared to the control group at the day 1–7, IFN-β levels were higher in moderate, severe, and critical subjects at the day 8–14 or >14 compared to the healthy control and themselves at the day 1–7.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true

Breaking it down:
- "Recovered cases" → So the context is about cases that have recovered.
- "Within a few hours of virus entry" → The time frame is shortly after the virus enters the body.
- "Both α and β IFNs are rapidly produced" → Both IFNα and IFNβ are produced quickly.
- "An antiviral state is soon reached" → The body starts to produce antiviral effects, which is the result of the IFNs being produced.

The initial STL statement was:
globally[0,∞](IFNα(t)=c(high) and IFNβ(t) > c(high))

But the problem is that this only ensures that IFNα and IFNβ are at high levels for all time, which might not capture the rapid production and the timing of the antiviral state.

So, the key points to address are:
1. The time frame is within a few hours after virus entry. The original statement mentions "within a few hrs of virus entry," so the STL should reflect that the production happens in a short time window.
2. The production is "rapidly" produced, which implies that the levels are increasing quickly. The current STL uses "is close to high" which might not capture the rate of increase.
3. The antiviral state is reached "soon," so there's a temporal aspect where the antiviral effect occurs after the IFNs are produced.

Looking at the rules, the derivative terms are important. The original statement mentions that both IFNs are produced rapidly. So, their derivatives should be greater than zero, indicating an increase over time.

The initial STL uses "is" for the levels, but the correct approach would be to use derivative_greater_than to indicate the rate of change. Also, the time frame is from the moment of virus entry, which is when the production starts.

u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is

predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval

	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days

By day 14, we detected no viral reads for SARS-CoV-2, and the observed cytokines returned to baseline, with the exception of IL-6 and IL1RN or IL1RA, which remained elevated, similar to results observed with MERS (Pascal et al., 2015; Figures 3B and 3C).

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.

thinking prompt: Give an explanation of how you would translate the following natural language sentence into a signal temporal logic (STL) statement:
By day 14, we detected no viral reads for SARS-CoV-2, and the observed cytokines returned to baseline, with the exception of IL-6 and IL1RN or IL1RA, which remained elevated, similar to results observed with MERS (Pascal et al., 2015; Figures 3B and 3C).

What parts of the sentence make sense to translate and what parts don't? Think carefully, step-by-step through the process, and tell us about how STL could be used to capture the original semantic meaning of the natural language sentence.

Your STL response must conform to the following rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | is | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_is
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than c
is : s(t) = c # Species s is close to c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change of species s is greater than d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than d_c
derivative_is : d_s(t) = d_c # The rate of change species s is close to d_c
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
predicate : u | u1 and u2 | u1 implies u2 # You can combine predicates with Boolean operators
temporal_operator : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(predicate) # This means that between day t_a and t_b, there is a point when the predicate becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means the predicate is true over the entire interval from day t_a to t_b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This means there is at least 1 time between days t_a and t_b that the predicate is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Time in days
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # Species names you can use
d_s : d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # Names for derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.
